clinicalPearls: A benign fibroblastic and myofibroblastic proliferation of the palmar (Dupuytren) or plantar (Ledderhose) aponeurosis
Palmar disease typically affects the ring and little finger rays, progressing from nodules to cords and ultimately a fixed flexion contracture
It is commonest in older men of Northern European ancestry and is associated with diabetes, alcohol, smoking, antiepileptic use, and manual labour
Plantar fibromatosis produces firm nodules in the arch of the foot but far less often leads to contracture than its palmar counterpart
A strong diathesis is suggested by early onset, bilateral disease, knuckle pads (Garrod pads), and coexistent plantar or penile (Peyronie) fibromatosis
Microscopically there are cellular fascicles of bland myofibroblasts, many showing nuclear beta-catenin expression
Early or non-contractile disease is managed conservatively, with needle aponeurotomy, collagenase injection, or fasciectomy reserved for functionally limiting contracture
Recurrence after intervention is common, reflecting the field nature of the disease
reference.pathophysiology: Superficial fibromatosis is a benign but locally persistent proliferation of myofibroblasts within the palmar or plantar aponeurosis. The process evolves through a proliferative phase of cellular nodules, an involutional phase in which myofibroblasts align and contract, and a residual phase of dense, relatively acellular collagen forming cords. Myofibroblast contraction, mediated by their smooth muscle-like contractile apparatus and by remodelling of the surrounding collagen, produces the progressive flexion deformity that characterises palmar disease. Dysregulated Wnt and beta-catenin signalling, together with profibrotic growth factors, is implicated in driving the proliferation, and many lesions show nuclear beta-catenin. A genetic predisposition interacts with metabolic and lifestyle factors such as diabetes, alcohol, and smoking, explaining the familial clustering and the recognised disease associations.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath
Callus, plantar fibroma mimics, or foreign body granuloma in the foot
Epithelioid sarcoma or other soft tissue malignancy in atypical cases
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination including the tabletop test for palmar contracture
Goniometric measurement of joint contracture to monitor progression
Ultrasound or MRI to define nodules and cords when the picture is atypical
Histology in resected specimens to confirm the diagnosis and exclude a deep fibromatosis or sarcoma
Assessment for associated knuckle pads and plantar or penile involvement
Screening for associated conditions such as diabetes where clinically indicated
redFlags: Rapid growth, pain, or a deep or fixed mass suggesting deep fibromatosis or malignancy
Severe progressive contracture threatening hand function
Atypical location or appearance not fitting classic palmar or plantar disease
Recurrent or aggressive disease after multiple interventions
reference.prognosis: Superficial fibromatosis is benign and does not metastasise, but it is often progressive and recurrent, and palmar disease in particular can cause substantial functional disability from fixed contracture. Outcome after treatment depends on disease severity and the strength of the underlying diathesis, with recurrence being frequent.
pitfalls: Mistaking a palmar or plantar nodule for a ganglion or a soft tissue sarcoma
Intervening too early before a functionally significant contracture has developed
Underestimating the high recurrence rate when counselling patients before surgery
Failing to recognise a strong diathesis and its implications for prognosis and recurrence
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Observe mild, non-progressive disease with periodic goniometric assessment, reserving intervention for functionally significant contracture
Treat progressive palmar (Dupuytren) contracture with percutaneous needle aponeurotomy, collagenase injection or surgical fasciectomy
Consider radiotherapy in early proliferative nodular disease to slow progression
Manage plantar (Ledderhose) disease with cushioning orthotics, padding and physiotherapy, reserving surgery for refractory cases
Provide postprocedural hand therapy and night splinting to maintain extension
Address associated factors such as diabetes, alcohol and smoking, and counsel on the high recurrence risk where a strong diathesis exists
Refer to a hand surgeon for assessment when contracture limits function
